title: Lava and Kusha
hook: Valmiki takes Sita in, and teaches her twin sons to sing the Ramayana
carry: the ramayana lives by being sung
tomorrow: Sita goes home to the earth

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Uttara Kanda opened. Gossip reached the king, and Lakshmana left Sita by the Ganga. Your line was dharma is subtle, and may be questioned. Today, two boys are born in a hermitage.

Sita doesn't stay alone on the riverbank for long. Young hermits find her weeping and run to tell their teacher, and he comes down to the water himself. It's Valmiki, the poet, the man who, at the very start of this serial, heard a bird's cry and found the first verse. He takes Sita by the hand and walks her to the women of the hermitage. The poet of the story has just stepped into it.
screen: `THE HERMITS FIND HER.` → `VALMIKI COMES DOWN TO THE WATER.` → `THE POET STEPS INTO THE STORY.`

segments.voice: Valmiki tells Sita he knows she's done nothing wrong, and gives her a home among the hermit women. Months later, she gives birth to twins. Valmiki prepares protective rites for the newborns with kusha grass, the sacred grass of Vedic ritual. The elder is touched with the tops of the grass, so he is Kusha; the younger with the lower part, the lava, so he is Lava. Then Valmiki folds the whole poem back on itself. As the boys grow, he teaches them the Ramayana: this very song, with their father as its hero. They learn it by heart and sing it beautifully. Years later, Rama holds a great horse sacrifice, the ashvamedha. Valmiki brings the boys, and they sing the poem in the open, day after day. Crowds gather. Rama hears it, is moved, and doesn't yet know whose sons are singing. The poem's very first book opens with Kusha and Lava singing it before Rama, so the frame was this moment all along. Here's the teaching. The Ramayana was made to be sung and heard, and Hindus still keep it that way: a grandmother singing over the stove, a Ram katha at the temple that runs for days, the Ramlila plays at Dussehra, a family reading a chapter aloud together. Hearing sacred stories, shravana, is counted as a form of devotion in itself. And the first people to carry this one were two children who learned it by heart.
screen: `VALMIKI TAKES SITA IN.` · `KUSHA AND LAVA: NAMED FOR GRASS.` · `THE SONS LEARN THEIR FATHER'S STORY.` · `SHRAVANA: HEARING IS DEVOTION.` · then, large: `A STORY MADE TO BE SUNG.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus sing a simple line for Rama: Sri Ram, Jai Ram, Jai Jai Ram. Say it or sing it softly, slowly, for two minutes, and listen to your own voice the way the crowd listened to the twins. If you don't pray, hum a song someone in your family taught you, and notice who you learned it from.

Kusha, Sita's son, named for the tip of the sacred grass used at his birth rite. With his twin Lava, he grows up in Valmiki's hermitage, learns his father's story, and sings it before him without knowing.
Your line: the Ramayana lives by being sung. Two boys carried it first. That's the week. Rest well.
